Mission 1

Mission 1: Paul's angriest letter is about whether new believers must be circumcised. Why did that matter so much?

Make a guess: Paul's angriest letter is about whether new believers must be circumcised. Why did that matter so much?

Mission 1

Who were "the Galatians"?

  • Galatia: (1) the old ethnic territory of Celtic Galatians in central Anatolia (Ancyra, modern Ankara); (2) the larger Roman province of Galatia, which also included Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe.
  • South Galatian theory: Paul writes to the churches of the First Journey (Acts 13–14). Supported by W. M. Ramsay; it fits your spec ("following the First Missionary Journey"). Date: perhaps c. AD 48–49, or the early 50s.
  • North Galatian theory: ethnic Galatia, visited on the second and third journeys (16:6; 18:23). J. B. Lightfoot (1828–1889) held this; dated in the mid-50s.
  • The readers are mostly Gentile converts (4:8: they once served "those who by nature are not gods").
  • Paul first preached there "because of weakness in the flesh" (4:13): probably an illness; they received him "as an angel of God" (4:14).
Mission 1

The crisis (1:6–9)

  • No thanksgiving, unlike Paul's other letters. Instead: "I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different 'good news'" (Galatians 1:6, WEBBE).
  • "There are some who trouble you" (1:7): Jewish-Christian teachers, often called Judaizers (some scholars prefer "the agitators" or "the teachers").
  • Their demands: circumcision (5:2; 6:12), the Jewish calendar ("You observe days, months, seasons, and years", 4:10), probably food laws (2:12).
  • Their likely charge (inferred from Paul's replies, 1:1, 10–12): Paul is a second-hand apostle who dropped the Law to make conversion easy.
  • "Even though we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you any 'good news' other than that which we preached to you, let him be cursed." (Galatians 1:8, WEBBE)
Mission 1

Paul's defence (1:10–2:21)

  • Source: "I didn't receive it from man, nor was I taught it, but it came to me through revelation of Jesus Christ." (Galatians 1:12, WEBBE)
  • Story: zealous persecutor (1:13–14); called (1:15–16); Arabia and Damascus; after three years, fifteen days with Peter (1:18).
  • Jerusalem after fourteen years (2:1–10): Titus, "being a Greek", is not made to be circumcised (2:3); James, Cephas and John give "the right hand of fellowship" (2:9).
  • Antioch (2:11–14): Peter eats with Gentiles, then withdraws when "some people came from James"; "I resisted him to his face" (2:11).
  • Conclusion (2:15–21): justification by faith; "I have been crucified with Christ… Christ lives in me" (2:20); "if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing!" (2:21).
Mission 1Read the source

Not by works of the law

> "…knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, even we believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by the works of the law, because no flesh will be justified by the works of the law." (Galatians 2:16, WEBBE)

  • Justified (dikaioō): declared or put right with God; a law-court and covenant word.
  • Works of the law: doing what the Torah requires; in Galatia, especially circumcision, food laws and calendar.

Q1 Who are "we" in 2:16?

Show answer

Jewish believers such as Paul and Peter (2:15): even Jews are justified by faith.

Q2 Why does this answer the Antioch incident?

Show answer

If Jews and Gentiles are justified the same way, separating at table denies the gospel.

Quick check
?Why does Paul tell the story of his visits to Jerusalem in Galatians 1–2?
Mission 1

Justification by faith (3:1–14)

  • Experience: "Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by hearing of faith?" (Galatians 3:2, WEBBE)
  • Abraham: "believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness" (3:6, quoting Genesis 15:6). Those of faith are Abraham's children; "in you all the nations will be blessed" (3:8).
  • Curse: the Law curses all who do not "continue in all things" (3:10, Deuteronomy 27:26). "The righteous will live by faith" (3:11, Habakkuk 2:4).
  • Exchange: "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us" (3:13), quoting Deuteronomy 21:23, "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree".
  • Aim: "that the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Christ Jesus" (3:14).
Mission 1

Then why the Law? (3:15–4:7)

  • Promise first: the covenant with Abraham came 430 years before the Law; the Law "does not annul" it (3:17).
  • "Then why is there the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come" (Galatians 3:19, WEBBE): temporary, for a period.
  • "The law has become our tutor to bring us to Christ… now that faith has come, we are no longer under a tutor." (3:24–25) Tutor (paidagōgos): the slave who guarded a child until adulthood.
  • "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus." (Galatians 3:28, WEBBE)
  • Adoption: God sent his Son "born under the law" to redeem, and the Spirit crying "Abba, Father!" (4:4–6). From slaves to heirs.
  • Then an allegory: Hagar and Sarah, slavery and freedom (4:21–31).
Mission 1Diversity

What did Paul mean?

  • Reformation reading: Martin Luther (1483–1546), Commentary on Galatians (1535): faith alone, not human effort or merit, makes a sinner right with God; the Law shows sin.
  • Catholic teaching (Council of Trent, 1547): justification is a gift received in faith that also renews the person; faith works through love (5:6). The Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (Lutheran World Federation and Catholic Church, 1999) found a shared basic understanding.
  • New Perspective: E. P. Sanders (1937–2022), Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977): Judaism was not a religion of earning salvation but of grace and covenant (covenantal nomism). James D. G. Dunn (1939–2020) named "the New Perspective on Paul" (1983): "works of the law" are chiefly boundary markers (circumcision, food, Sabbath) separating Jew from Gentile.
  • "Faith in" or "faithfulness of" Christ? The Greek pistis Christou (2:16) can mean either; e.g. Richard B. Hays, The Faith of Jesus Christ (1983), argued for "faithfulness of".
  • Paul is arguing with fellow Jewish believers about Gentiles; Galatians is not a verdict on Judaism as a faith.
Quick check
?According to James Dunn's "New Perspective", what are "works of the law" in Galatians mainly about?
Mission 1

Christian freedom (5:1–15)

  • "Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don't be entangled again with a yoke of bondage." (Galatians 5:1, WEBBE)
  • Circumcision as a requirement would mean "Christ will profit you nothing" (5:2); "neither circumcision nor uncircumcision amounts to anything, but faith working through love" (5:6).
  • "Only don't use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love be servants to one another." (Galatians 5:13, WEBBE)
  • "The whole law is fulfilled in one word… 'You shall love your neighbour as yourself.'" (5:14, Leviticus 19:18)
  • Freedom from the Law's yoke is freedom for love, not licence.
Mission 1

Life in the Spirit: a code for living (5:16–6:10)

  • "Walk by the Spirit, and you won't fulfil the lust of the flesh." (5:16) Flesh: human nature turned in on itself, not just the body.
  • Works of the flesh (5:19–21): sexual immorality, idolatry, sorcery, hatred, strife, jealousies, anger, divisions, envy, drunkenness…
  • "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law." (Galatians 5:22–23, WEBBE)
  • Community: restore gently (6:1); "Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." (6:2)
  • Sowing and reaping (6:7–8); "let's do what is good towards all men" (6:10).
  • Note the lists: Paul does give a code, but rooted in the Spirit, not in Torah observance.
Mission 1

Value for the Early Church

  • Gentile inclusion: Gentiles join without becoming Jews; the same issue as the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15) and Peter's vision.
  • One table: Jews and Gentiles eat together; unity is a gospel issue (2:11–14; 3:28).
  • Authority: shows how the early church tested teaching and leaders (1:8–9; 2:9).
  • Ethics without the Law: a pattern for Gentile churches: Spirit, love, community discipline.
  • Earliest witness: possibly Paul's earliest letter; gives a first-hand account of Paul's life (1–2) beside Acts.
  • Later influence: central to the Reformation; Galatians 3:28 cited in later arguments about slavery and the equality of women and men.
Mission 1Evaluate

Freedom or code?

  • Claim: Galatians is more about freedom than about rules for living.
  • Freedom: "for freedom" (5:1, 13); against circumcision rules and calendars; the Spirit, not a written code, guides.
  • Code: clear lists of vices and virtues (5:19–23); warnings that wrongdoers "will not inherit God's Kingdom" (5:21); practical commands (6:1–10).
  • Both: freedom is the setting; love is the rule (5:13–14). Augustine's later "Love, and do what you will" reflects this logic (Homilies on 1 John 7.8).
  • Concerns: risk of antinomianism (ignoring moral law); Paul says the Law is not against the promise (3:21); James 2:24 says justification is "not only by faith": tension or different questions?
  • Today: Christians differ over how far biblical codes (e.g. on sexuality or Sabbath) bind; Galatians is used on several sides.
  • Judgement criteria: what "law" means in each verse; is a code compatible with freedom; how does one judge what the Spirit leads to?
Mission check

?A new church in a different culture is told by visiting teachers that converts must adopt the visitors' customs of diet and dress before they are full members. Which argument from Galatians would Paul most likely use?

For Paul, the question "who may eat together?" is the question "how is anyone right with God?". Next: a divided church at Corinth.

Mission 2

Mission 2: If God accepts you before you do anything good, why bother being good at all?

Make a guess: If God accepts you before you do anything good, why bother being good at all?

Mission 2

The question: how is a sinner put right with God?

  • Justification: being put right (made or declared righteous) before God. From Greek dikaioō, "to justify, acquit".
  • Christians agree: all have sinned (Romans 3:23), and God's grace saves through Christ.
  • They have disagreed on how: by faith alone? By faith and works? Who decides who is saved?
  • 1517: Martin Luther (1483–1546), an Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg, posts the 95 Theses against the sale of indulgences.
  • The quarrel over indulgences became a quarrel over justification: the heart of the Reformation.
  • The same words ("justified", "faith", "works of the law") are at the centre of Galatians (see Mission 1).
Mission 2Read the source

Luther's key texts

> "For in it is revealed God's righteousness from faith to faith. As it is written, 'But the righteous shall live by faith.'" (Romans 1:17, WEBBE)

> "Being therefore justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ" (Romans 5:1, WEBBE)

> "for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast." (Ephesians 2:8–9, WEBBE)

> "a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ" (Galatians 2:16, WEBBE)

Q1 In Ephesians 2:8–9, why are works excluded?

Show answer

Salvation is God's gift, so no one can boast of earning it.

Q2 Which verse links justification with peace with God?

Show answer

Romans 5:1.

  • Galatians 2:16 is the thesis of the letter; Paul backs it with Habakkuk 2:4 in Galatians 3:11.
Mission 2

So why be good?

  • Reformers' answer: good works do not make us righteous; they follow from being made right, as fruit follows from a good tree (Matthew 7:17).
  • Luther, The Freedom of a Christian (1520): a Christian is free from the need to earn salvation, and so free to serve the neighbour in love (paraphrase).
  • "We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works" (Ephesians 2:10).
  • Calvin: faith alone justifies, yet the faith that justifies is never alone; it always brings a new life (sanctification) (Antidote to Trent, 1547, paraphrase).
  • Galatians: what counts is "faith working through love" (Galatians 5:6); freedom is for serving one another (5:13).
Mission 2Evaluate

Do the New Testament letters support faith alone?

  • Claim: The New Testament letters support justification by faith alone.
  • For: Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16; Ephesians 2:8–9 contrast faith with works directly.
  • For: Paul's model is Abraham, counted righteous by believing before he was circumcised (Romans 4:3, 4:10).
  • Against: "Alone" is not in Paul's Greek; Luther added it (allein) when he translated Romans 3:28 into German.
  • Against: James 2:24 says "not only by faith"; Paul too says God will "pay back to everyone according to their works" (Romans 2:6).
  • Against: "Works of the law" may mean Jewish law-observance, not good deeds in general (see Mission 3).
  • Judge it by: What does Paul mean by "works"? Can James and Paul be reconciled? Is Luther's reading shaped by his own struggle?
Mission check

?A student says: "If I'm saved by faith alone, I can live however I like." Which reply would both Luther and Calvin give?

For the Reformers, good conduct is the result of being put right with God, not the route to it. Part 2: the Catholic answer at Trent, and Sanders.

Mission 3

Mission 3: Did the Reformers misread Paul, and do Catholics really think good deeds earn heaven?

Make a guess: Did the Reformers misread Paul, and do Catholics really think good deeds earn heaven?

Mission 3

Sanders: what was first-century Judaism really like?

  • E. P. Sanders (1937–2022), Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977).
  • Many Protestant scholars had pictured Judaism as legalism: earning salvation by piling up good works. Paul was read as Luther against medieval Catholicism.
  • Sanders studied the Jewish sources (rabbinic writings, Dead Sea Scrolls, Apocrypha) and found a different pattern: covenantal nomism.
  • Getting in: by grace. God chose Israel and made the covenant; no one earned it.
  • Staying in: by obedience to the Law (nomos), with God's provision of repentance and atonement for failure.
  • So works were the response to grace and the condition of remaining in the covenant, not the way to earn it.
Mission 3

Sanders on Paul and works

  • If Judaism was not legalism, what was Paul's problem? Sanders (paraphrase): not that Jews tried to earn salvation, but that salvation is now in Christ, for Jews and Gentiles alike.
  • Sanders' own summary: "this is what Paul finds wrong in Judaism: it is not Christianity" (1977, p. 552).
  • The question was entry: must Gentiles become Jews to belong? Paul: no; membership is by faith in Christ.
  • James D. G. Dunn developed this: "Works of the law" in Galatians are the Law as the marker of who belongs: circumcision, food laws, Sabbath (see Galatians 2:11–16, the meal at Antioch).
  • Yet for Paul too, believers will be judged by their works (Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10). Works are the condition of staying in, not of getting in (paraphrase of Sanders).
  • This "New Perspective on Paul" (name from Dunn, 1983) was developed by Dunn and N. T. Wright.
Mission 3Read the source

The meal at Antioch

> "For before some people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision." (Galatians 2:12, WEBBE)

> "yet knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ" (Galatians 2:16, WEBBE)

Q1 What practice is at issue just before Paul's statement about justification?

Show answer

Whether Jewish believers may eat with Gentile believers: table fellowship.

Q2 How does that context support the New Perspective reading of "works of the law"?

Show answer

The dispute is about the Law marking who belongs, not about earning God's favour.

Mission 3Diversity

Where the churches stand now

  • 1999: the Lutheran World Federation and the Catholic Church signed the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (Augsburg, 31 October).
  • Core agreement: we are accepted "by grace alone, in faith in Christ's saving work", and the Spirit renews hearts and calls to good works (§15, short quotation).
  • The mutual condemnations of the 1500s are said not to apply to the teaching of the other side as set out in the Declaration.
  • Later joined by the World Methodist Council (2006), the World Communion of Reformed Churches (2017); the Anglican Communion welcomed and affirmed it (2016–17).
  • Differences remain: merit, the role of sacraments, how far a believer is "righteous and sinner" at once. Some Lutherans and evangelicals reject the Declaration.
  • Orthodox Christians frame salvation more as theosis (sharing God's life) than as a courtroom verdict.
  • Critics of Sanders (e.g. Stephen Westerholm, Perspectives Old and New on Paul, 2004) argue the "Lutheran" Paul is still right.
Mission 3

Why good conduct matters in each view

  • Catholic (Trent): works done in grace grow and keep justification; mortal sin can lose it.
  • Lutheran: works are the fruit of faith and serve the neighbour; they add nothing to justification.
  • Reformed (Calvin): works are the evidence of a living faith and of election; they give a secondary assurance.
  • New Perspective (Sanders, Dunn, Wright): believers will be judged by their works, which show they are "in Christ".
  • Methodist (Wesley): faith leads to growing holiness of heart and life.
  • In every view, good conduct is required of a Christian. The disagreement is about why.
  • Galatians 5:22: the "fruit of the Spirit" is the life Paul expects of the justified.
  • Trent (1547): faith is the beginning of salvation; works without faith do not justify; justification lost by mortal sin can be restored through grace in penance.
Mission 3Evaluate

Are faith and works both aspects of justification?

  • Claim: Both faith and works are aspects of justification.
  • For: James 2:24; Romans 2:6; Matthew 25:31–46: judgement looks at deeds.
  • For: Trent and the 1999 Declaration both link faith to a changed life.
  • For: Sanders too: for Paul, believers are judged by their works.
  • Against: Romans 3:28, Galatians 2:16, Ephesians 2:8–9: faith apart from works.
  • Against: If works count, assurance is lost: no one knows if they have done enough (Luther's experience).
  • Middle position: faith alone justifies; works follow necessarily. Does that make works an aspect, or only a result?
  • Judge it by: What does "works" mean (moral deeds or Torah observance)? Is justification a moment or a process? Does the answer fit Paul and James?
Mission check

?Two Christians are discussing a friend who has stopped believing but still volunteers at a food bank every week. Which statement fits the Council of Trent's teaching?

Trent: grace first, faith as beginning, works done in grace as growth. Every tradition requires good conduct; they differ on why.

Mission 4

Mission 4: A church split into fan clubs for its favourite preachers. How did Paul try to bring it back together?

Make a guess: A church split into fan clubs for its favourite preachers. How did Paul try to bring it back together?

Mission 4

Roman Corinth

  • Old Greek Corinth was destroyed by Rome in 146 BC; Julius Caesar refounded it as a Roman colony in 44 BC, settled largely by freedmen.
  • Capital of the province of Achaia; on the isthmus between two ports, Lechaeum (west) and Cenchreae (east): trade, travellers, wealth.
  • Host of the Isthmian Games; many temples and cults; a Jewish synagogue (Acts 18:4).
  • A city where status could be won: new money, patrons and clients, public honour, admired speakers.
  • Its reputation for vice is partly old Greek slander; Strabo's famous claim of a thousand temple prostitutes refers to the pre-146 BC city and is doubted by historians.
Mission 4

Founding and the letters

  • Second journey (Acts 18:1–18): Paul works with Aquila and Priscilla, tentmakers expelled from Rome (18:2–3). Crispus, synagogue ruler, believes "with all his house" (18:8).
  • Paul stays "a year and six months" (18:11); Gallio dismisses the case against him (18:12–17).
  • Apollos, "an Alexandrian… an eloquent man… mighty in the Scriptures" (18:24), later works in Corinth (19:1).
  • 1 Corinthians is written from Ephesus ("I will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost", 16:8), c. AD 53–55, on the third journey.
  • Paul had written before (5:9). Now he answers oral reports ("those who are from Chloe's household", 1:11) and a letter from them ("Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me", 7:1).
Mission 4

A church full of problems

  • Factions around leaders (chs 1–4).
  • Sexual immorality: a man with his father's wife (ch. 5); visiting prostitutes (6:12–20).
  • Lawsuits between believers (6:1–11).
  • Marriage and celibacy questions (ch. 7); food offered to idols (chs 8–10).
  • Worship: head coverings; rich and poor divided at the Lord's Supper (ch. 11); rivalry over spiritual gifts, especially tongues (chs 12–14).
  • Resurrection denied by some (ch. 15); the collection for Jerusalem (16:1–4).
  • Common root: pride in status, knowledge and spiritual gifts. Paul's thesis comes first: "that there be no divisions amongst you" (1:10).
Mission 4

"I follow Paul…"

  • "Each one of you says, 'I follow Paul,' 'I follow Apollos,' 'I follow Cephas,' and, 'I follow Christ.'" (1 Corinthians 1:12, WEBBE)
  • Paul: founder. Apollos: eloquent, perhaps admired by those who prized wisdom. Cephas (Peter): perhaps for Jewish believers, or those who prized the Twelve. "Christ": perhaps a super-spiritual group, or Paul's own sarcastic retort; scholars disagree.
  • These are probably not formal parties with doctrines, but loyalties: people attached to the leader who baptised or impressed them (1:14–16).
  • Ancient cities had rival followers of teachers and patrons; the church copied the culture.
Mission 4Read the source

Is Christ divided?

> "Now I beg you, brothers, through the name of our Lord, Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions amongst you, but that you be perfected together in the same mind and in the same judgement." (1 Corinthians 1:10, WEBBE)

> "Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptised into the name of Paul?" (1 Corinthians 1:13, WEBBE)

  • Divisions (schismata): tears in a garment; source of the English "schism".
  • Margaret M. Mitchell, Paul and the Rhetoric of Reconciliation (1991), reads the whole letter as an appeal for concord, with 1:10 as its thesis.

Q1 Which three questions in 1:13 show the factions are absurd?

Show answer

Christ divided? Paul crucified for you? Baptised in Paul's name?

Q2 Why does Paul name himself rather than only his rivals?

Show answer

To show he rejects even his own fan club: the problem is loyalty to people, not to the wrong person.

Quick check
?What were the "divisions" in Corinth described in 1 Corinthians 1:10–17 mainly about?
Mission 4

The wisdom of the cross (1:18–2:16)

  • "The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are dying, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God." (1 Corinthians 1:18, WEBBE)
  • "Jews ask for signs, Greeks seek after wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Greeks" (1:22–23).
  • Look at yourselves: "not many are wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, and not many noble" (1:26); God chose the foolish and weak "that he might put to shame those who are wise" (1:27).
  • Look at me: "I didn't come with excellence of speech or of wisdom" (2:1); "not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power" (2:4).
  • True wisdom is God's, revealed by the Spirit (2:6–16).
  • Logic: if the gospel is a crucified Messiah, boasting about status or eloquence is out of place.
Mission 4

Servants, a field, a temple (3:1–4:21)

  • Babies: "I fed you with milk, not with solid food" (3:2); "jealousy, strife, and factions" show they are still "fleshly" (3:3).
  • Farm: "I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase." (1 Corinthians 3:6, WEBBE) Leaders are "God's fellow workers" (3:9).
  • Building: "no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ" (3:11); each builder's work will be tested (3:12–15).
  • Temple: "Don't you know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit lives in you?" (3:16) Here "you" is plural: the church together.
  • Stewards: "Christ's servants and stewards of God's mysteries" (4:1). "What do you have that you didn't receive?" (4:7)
  • Irony and appeal: "You are already filled… We are fools for Christ's sake" (4:8–10); "I became your father" (4:15); "be imitators of me" (4:16); "Shall I come to you with a rod, or in love…?" (4:21)
Mission 4

Teaching shaped for its audience

  • Status-conscious hearers: Paul turns honour upside down: weak, foolish, low (1:26–28); apostles "dishonour" (4:10).
  • Rhetoric-lovers: Corinth admired polished orators; Paul refuses "excellence of speech" (2:1) yet writes skilfully.
  • Mixed church: Gerd Theissen (b. 1943), The Social Setting of Pauline Christianity (English 1982), argued the church mixed a few wealthy patrons with many poor members, and many conflicts reflect that gap (e.g. 11:17–34).
  • Spiritual elitists: they claim wisdom and knowledge; Paul calls them "babies" (3:1).
  • Images from their city: building contractors, temples, farming, household stewards, the father of a family.
  • Result: unity is not uniformity; it rests on Christ as foundation and God as owner of the church ("you are Christ's", 3:23).
Quick check
?What is Paul's main point in the image "I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase" (1 Corinthians 3:6)?
Mission 4Evaluate

Can Paul's teaching unite divided churches today?

  • Claim: Paul's teaching on unity in 1 Corinthians 1–4 is an effective answer to division in churches today.
  • For: the core principle (one foundation, leaders as servants, no boasting) applies anywhere; the ecumenical movement often cites "Is Christ divided?" (1:13).
  • For: many modern splits are about personalities and celebrity preachers, very like Corinth.
  • Against: today's divisions are often about doctrine and authority (e.g. papacy, sacraments, ordination), which "speak the same thing" (1:10) cannot settle alone.
  • Against: Paul himself uses his authority strongly (4:21; 5:3); his solution relies on an apostle whom all respect.
  • Different views: some value diversity of traditions as healthy; others seek visible, structural unity; others a spiritual unity beneath differences.
  • Judgement criteria: what kind of unity (same mind, same structure, mutual respect)? What causes the division? Who has authority to resolve it?
Mission check

?A student society splits into followers of two popular online speakers. Each side mocks the other's speaker as less clever. Which response best applies Paul's teaching in 1 Corinthians 1–4?

Paul's answer to factions is the cross and a humble view of leaders. Next: how he answers Corinth's moral and worship problems.

Mission 5

Mission 5: "All things are lawful for me," said the Corinthians. What was Paul's answer?

Make a guess: "All things are lawful for me," said the Corinthians. What was Paul's answer?

Mission 5

A scandal tolerated (5:1–13)

  • Recall: a status-proud, divided church (see Mission 4).
  • "One has his father's wife" (5:1): probably his stepmother. Leviticus 18:8 and Roman law both forbade it. The church is "arrogant" rather than grieving (5:2).
  • Paul's verdict: "deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus" (1 Corinthians 5:5, WEBBE): exclusion from the community, with restoration as the aim.
  • Yeast: "a little yeast leavens the whole lump"; "Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed" (5:6–7). Sin tolerated spreads.
  • Insiders, not outsiders: "Don't you judge those who are within?… those who are outside, God judges." (5:12–13) Paul does not ask them to leave the world (5:10).
Mission 5

"All things are lawful" (6:12–20)

  • Paul quotes Corinthian slogans and answers them:
  • "'All things are lawful for me,' but not all things are expedient. 'All things are lawful for me,' but I will not be brought under the power of anything." (1 Corinthians 6:12, WEBBE)
  • "'Foods for the belly, and the belly for foods'" (6:13): they treated the body as morally unimportant. Paul: "the body is not for sexual immorality, but for the Lord".
  • The body will be raised (6:14); bodies are "members of Christ" (6:15); sex unites two as "one flesh" (6:16, Genesis 2:24).
  • "Flee sexual immorality!" (6:18)
  • Behind this: a view, common in Greek thought, that what you do with the body does not touch the soul.
Mission 5Read the source

Not your own

> "Or don't you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God's." (1 Corinthians 6:19–20, WEBBE)

  • In 3:16 the church is God's temple; here the individual body is.
  • "Bought with a price": the language of buying a slave's freedom; the price is Christ's death.

Q1 Which Corinthian assumption do these verses deny?

Show answer

That the body does not matter morally: it belongs to God and houses the Spirit.

Q2 Name one modern ethical debate where Christians use these verses.

Show answer

E.g. sexual ethics, drug use, self-harm, care of health: applied variously.

Mission 5

Marriage and singleness (ch. 7)

  • "Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman." (7:1) Many scholars think this is their slogan, which Paul qualifies.
  • Mutual duty: husband and wife each give the other "affection owed"; neither has sole authority over their own body (7:3–4): striking mutuality for its time.
  • Celibacy a gift: "I wish that all men were like me. However, each man has his own gift from God" (7:7).
  • Divorce: "not I, but the Lord": a wife should not leave, a husband not divorce (7:10–11, echoing Jesus' teaching). Mixed marriages: stay if the unbeliever is willing; "if the unbeliever departs, let there be separation" (7:12–15).
  • Stay as you were called (7:17–24): circumcised or not; a slave, but "if you get an opportunity to become free, use it" (7:21).
  • "The time is short" (7:29): "the distress that is on us" (7:26) shapes the advice to remain unmarried.
Quick check
?What is distinctive about Paul's teaching on marital duty in 1 Corinthians 7:3–4?
Mission 5

Food offered to idols (8:1–13; 10:14–11:1)

  • Much meat in Corinth's market had passed through a temple sacrifice; dinners were often held in temple dining rooms.
  • The "strong": "no idol is anything in the world, and… there is no other God but one" (8:4). Paul agrees, but: "Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up." (8:1)
  • The "weak": eating troubles their conscience. "Be careful that by no means does this liberty of yours become a stumbling block to the weak." (8:9) "If food causes my brother to stumble, I will eat no meat forever more" (8:13).
  • But no idol feasts: "flee from idolatry" (10:14); "You can't both drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons." (10:21)
  • Market meat is fine, "asking no question" (10:25), unless someone points out it was offered to idols (10:28).
  • Rule of thumb: "'All things are lawful for me,' but not all things build up" (10:23); "whatever you do, do all to the glory of God" (10:31); "Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ." (11:1)
Mission 5

Order in worship (11:2–34)

  • Head coverings (11:2–16): women "praying or prophesying" should cover their heads (11:5); argument from "head" (11:3), creation, nature and custom; "neither is the woman independent of the man, nor the man independent of the woman, in the Lord" (11:11).
  • Note: 11:5 assumes women pray and prophesy aloud in worship.
  • The Lord's Supper (11:17–34): "it is not the Lord's supper that you eat. For in your eating each one takes his own supper first. One is hungry, and another is drunken." (11:20–21)
  • The meal was probably eaten in a wealthy member's house; richer members ate early and well, the poor came late to little. "Do you despise God's assembly and put them to shame who don't have enough?" (11:22)
  • Whoever eats "in an unworthy way… doesn't discern the Lord's body" (11:29): often read as the body that is the church, as well as the bread.
  • "When you come together to eat, wait for one another." (11:33)
Mission 5Read the source

The earliest account of the Last Supper

> "Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me." (1 Corinthians 11:24, WEBBE)

> "This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink, in memory of me." (1 Corinthians 11:25, WEBBE)

> "For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes." (1 Corinthians 11:26, WEBBE)

  • "I received… I delivered" (11:23): words for handing on tradition: this was taught before the Gospels were written.

Q1 Why does Paul repeat the words of institution to a church with problems at its meal?

Show answer

To show the meal proclaims Christ's self-giving death; humiliating the poor contradicts it.

Q2 What three time-frames appear in 11:24–26?

Show answer

Past: "in memory"; present: "you proclaim"; future: "until he comes".

Mission 5

Gifts, love and order (12:1–14:40; 16:1–4)

  • "There are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit" (12:4), given "for the profit of all" (12:7).
  • One body: "In one Spirit we were all baptised into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether bond or free" (12:13); "The eye can't tell the hand, 'I have no need for you'" (12:21).
  • Love (ch. 13): without love, tongues are "sounding brass or a clanging cymbal" (13:1). "The greatest of these is love." (13:13)
  • Tongues and prophecy (ch. 14): prophecy "edifies the assembly" (14:4); "five words with my understanding" rather than ten thousand in a tongue (14:19); tongues need interpretation.
  • "Let the wives be quiet in the assemblies" (14:34–35): much debated. "Let all things be done decently and in order." (14:40)
  • Collection (16:1–4): "On the first day of every week, let each one of you save as he may prosper" (16:2), for poor believers in Jerusalem.
Quick check
?What is Paul's main reason for placing the chapter on love (ch. 13) between the chapters on spiritual gifts?
Mission 5Diversity

How churches read these chapters today

  • Lord's Supper: Catholic and Orthodox churches: the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood (Mass; Divine Liturgy); Lutherans: real presence; many Reformed: spiritual presence; many Baptists and others: a memorial ("in memory of me").
  • Spiritual gifts: Pentecostal and charismatic churches practise tongues, prophecy and healing today; cessationists hold that such gifts ended with the apostles.
  • Women in worship (11:5; 14:34–35): complementarian churches restrict some roles; egalitarian churches ordain women and read 14:34–35 as local, or (with Gordon Fee) as a later insertion, since its position moves in some manuscripts.
  • Head coverings: kept in some traditions (e.g. some Brethren, Mennonite and Orthodox women); read as cultural by most.
  • Divorce: Catholic canon law's Pauline privilege draws on 7:15; Protestant churches vary on remarriage.
  • Church discipline (ch. 5): formal excommunication, pastoral exclusion, or rarely used.
Mission 5

Value for the Early Church

  • Practical pastoral theology: Paul applies the cross, the Spirit and the coming end to everyday questions (sex, food, meals, meetings).
  • Earliest evidence for Christian worship: the Lord's Supper words (11:23–26), gifts in worship, Sunday collection (16:2).
  • A method: freedom limited by love and by care for the weak; "not all things build up" (10:23).
  • Identity: how a Gentile church in a pagan city lives apart from idolatry without leaving the world (5:10; 10:25–27).
  • Unity across status: rich and poor at one table; Jew and Greek, slave and free in one body (12:13).
Mission 5Evaluate

Is Paul's moral teaching still relevant?

  • Claim: Paul's teaching on moral living and worship in 1 Corinthians is still relevant today.
  • Relevant: principles transfer: body as temple; love before rights; care for the weak conscience; no humiliation of the poor at worship; order and mutual edification.
  • Relevant: issues recur: sexual ethics, consumer choices with moral strings attached, celebrity culture in churches, inequality.
  • Limited: some advice depends on the expected nearness of the end ("the time is short", 7:29) or on Corinthian customs (head coverings).
  • Contested: teaching on women's silence and on sexuality is read very differently; critics see patriarchal assumptions, others a faithful pattern.
  • Method question: separate principle from application? Who decides which parts are cultural? Paul himself distinguishes "the Lord" and "I" (7:10, 12).
  • Judgement criteria: consistency with the letter's own centre (love, cross, building up); the reader's tradition (scripture, church teaching, reason, experience).
Mission check

?A Christian student knows that a party will be held at a club whose events fund a cause she believes is wrong. She is free to go, but a new Christian friend is troubled by it. Applying 1 Corinthians 8–10, what would Paul most likely advise?

In Corinth, freedom is real but limited by love, the body and the community. Next: Paul's letter to the Ephesians.

Mission 6

Mission 6: A letter from prison tells readers they are already seated in heaven. Why does it hand them armour?

Make a guess: A letter from prison tells readers they are already seated in heaven. Why does it hand them armour?

Mission 6

Ephesus and Paul's longest stay

  • Ephesus: chief city of the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey today); a port; home of the great Temple of Artemis.
  • Second journey: a brief visit, leaving Priscilla and Aquila there (Acts 18:19–21).
  • Third Missionary Journey: Paul returns. Three months in the synagogue (Acts 19:8), then two years teaching daily in the hall of Tyrannus (19:9–10).
  • Result: "all those who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus, both Jews and Greeks" (Acts 19:10).
  • Opposition: the silversmiths' riot led by Demetrius, whose trade in Artemis shrines was threatened (19:23–41).
  • Farewell to the Ephesian elders at Miletus: "for a period of three years I didn't cease to admonish everyone" (Acts 20:31).
Mission 6

The evidence: who wrote, and to whom?

  • The letter's own claim: from "Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus" (1:1), a "prisoner" (3:1; 4:1), "an ambassador in chains" (6:20). Carried by Tychicus (6:21).
  • Early use: accepted as Paul's from the second century. Tertullian reports that Marcion knew it as the letter "to the Laodiceans" (Against Marcion V.17).
  • The address: the words "at Ephesus" (1:1) are missing from the earliest manuscripts (the papyrus P46; the first hands of Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus).
  • No personal greetings, though Paul spent up to three years there; the writer has "heard" of their faith (1:15).
  • Close to Colossians: much shared wording; Tychicus' commission almost word for word (Ephesians 6:21–22; Colossians 4:7–8).
  • Style: very long sentences (1:3–14 is one sentence in Greek), many words not found in Paul's other letters.
Mission 6Evaluate

Did Paul write Ephesians?

  • Claim: Ephesians was written by Paul himself.
  • For: it names Paul twice (1:1; 3:1); the whole early church accepted it; a different scribe or a letter meant for several churches would explain the style and the missing greetings. F. F. Bruce (1910–1990) defended Paul's authorship (commentary on Colossians, Philemon and Ephesians, 1984).
  • Against: the dependence on Colossians looks like a later writer using it; salvation is described as already complete ("made us to sit with him in the heavenly places", 2:6), where Romans 6 keeps resurrection in the future; the "apostles and prophets" are a past foundation (2:20). E. J. Goodspeed (1871–1962, The Meaning of Ephesians, 1933) argued it was written by a disciple as a covering letter for a collection of Paul's letters.
  • A middle position: a circular letter from Paul to several churches of Asia, with the address left blank; Ephesus' copy gave it its name.
  • Judge it by: How much weight can style bear? Was pseudonymity (writing in a teacher's name) acceptable then? Does authorship change the letter's authority for the Church?
Quick check
?Which piece of evidence best supports the view that Ephesians was a circular letter to several churches?
Mission 6

Teacher, pastor, theologian

  • Chapters 1–3: what God has done (doctrine). Praise, prayer, the plan of salvation.
  • Chapters 4–6: how to live in response (practical advice). The hinge word: "I therefore… beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called" (4:1).
  • Scholars call this pattern indicative → imperative: the gift first, then the task.
  • Theologian: salvation, the Church as Christ's body, God's plan for the whole universe.
  • Teacher: explains the "mystery" now revealed (3:3–6).
  • Pastor: prays for the readers twice (1:15–23; 3:14–21); speaks to husbands, children, slaves and masters by name.
Mission 6Read the source

God's plan of salvation

> "even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we would be holy and without defect before him in love," (Ephesians 1:4, WEBBE)

> "to sum up all things in Christ, the things in the heavens and the things on the earth, in him." (Ephesians 1:10, WEBBE)

> "for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast." (Ephesians 2:8–9, WEBBE)

  • The plan runs from before creation (1:4) to the end of history (1:10). Redemption "through his blood" (1:7); the Spirit is the seal and down-payment (1:13–14).
  • Yet good works follow: "created in Christ Jesus for good works" (2:10).

Q1 According to 2:8–9, what is the source of salvation?

Show answer

God's grace, received through faith; not human works.

Q2 How wide is God's plan in 1:10?

Show answer

Everything in heaven and on earth, brought together under Christ.

Mission 6

One new humanity

  • Gentile readers were once "strangers" to Israel's covenants (2:12).
  • Christ "broke down the middle wall of separation" (2:14), to "create in himself one new man of the two, making peace" (2:15).
  • Background: a stone barrier in the Jerusalem Temple warned Gentiles, on pain of death, not to go further. (A warning inscription from it was found in 1871.)
  • Now: "fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God" (2:19), a temple built on Christ as cornerstone (2:20–22).
  • The mystery revealed to Paul: "the Gentiles are fellow heirs and fellow members of the body" (3:6).
  • For the Early Church: an answer to the biggest dispute of the age, whether Gentiles must become Jews first.
Mission 6Diversity

Chosen "in him": what does election mean?

  • Reformed (Calvinist): God chose particular individuals for salvation before creation (1:4–5), by grace alone, not foreseeing their merit.
  • Arminian and Wesleyan Protestants: God chose "in him": a people in Christ; individuals enter by faith, which they may freely accept or refuse.
  • Catholic and Orthodox: God's plan is to save all in Christ; grace is freely offered and human freedom must cooperate with it.
  • Karl Barth (1886–1968, Church Dogmatics II/2, 1942): Christ himself is the chosen one; humanity is chosen in him.
  • Common ground: the choice is God's initiative and its aim is holiness (1:4), not privilege.
Mission 6

Walking worthily: church and world

  • In the local church (4:1–16): keep "the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" (4:3).
  • Seven "ones": one body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, God and Father (4:4–6).
  • Christ gives gifts of people: apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds (pastors) and teachers (4:11), to build up the body to maturity (4:12–16).
  • In the world (4:17–5:20): no longer live as the Gentiles do (4:17). Put off the "old man", put on the "new man" (4:22–24).
  • Concrete: speak truth; "Be angry, and don't sin" (4:26); work, don't steal; kind speech; forgive "just as God also in Christ forgave you" (4:32).
  • "Walk in love" (5:2), as children of light (5:8); "be filled with the Spirit" in song and thanksgiving, not drunk with wine (5:18–20).
Mission 6

The household code

  • 5:21–6:9 follows the pattern of a household code (German Haustafel), as in Aristotle's Politics I: husband–wife, parent–child, master–slave.
  • Heading: "subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ" (5:21).
  • Wives: be subject to husbands "as to the Lord" (5:22). Husbands: love wives "even as Christ also loved the assembly and gave himself up for her" (5:25). Marriage pictures Christ and the Church (5:32).
  • Children: obey parents (6:1). Fathers: "don't provoke your children to wrath" (6:4).
  • Slaves: obey masters, as serving Christ (6:5). Masters: "give up threatening" (6:9); both have one Master in heaven.
  • New for its time: the weaker party is addressed directly as a moral agent; duties run both ways; Christ is the model of authority as self-giving.
Quick check
?Which statement about the household code in Ephesians 5:21–6:9 is accurate?
Mission 6Read the source

The armour of God

> "Put on the whole armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil." (Ephesians 6:11, WEBBE)

> "For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world's rulers of the darkness of this age, and against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places." (Ephesians 6:12, WEBBE)

  • Six pieces (6:14–17): belt of truth; breastplate of righteousness; shoes of the Good News of peace; shield of faith; helmet of salvation; sword of the Spirit, "the word of God". Then: prayer at all times (6:18).
  • Roots: in Isaiah, God himself wears righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation (Isaiah 59:17). Believers share God's own armour.
  • Mostly defensive: the command is to stand (6:11, 13, 14).

Q1 Who is the real enemy, according to 6:12?

Show answer

Spiritual powers of evil, not human beings.

Q2 Which piece of armour is also used to attack?

Show answer

The sword of the Spirit, God's word.

Mission 6Evaluate

Ephesians: valuable then, relevant now?

  • Value for the Early Church: a theology of one Church of Jews and Gentiles; a clear identity for converts from paganism; ethics that showed outsiders an orderly household; courage for a small minority against hostile "powers".
  • Relevant today, for: Christian unity (4:4–6 is often cited in ecumenical work); reconciliation across ethnic divides (2:14); marriage as self-giving love (5:25, read at many weddings); grace before works (2:8–9).
  • Questions today: the code's acceptance of slavery (later quoted by both slaveholders and abolitionists); complementarian Christians read 5:22–33 as a lasting pattern of roles in marriage, egalitarian Christians read 5:21 (mutual submission) as the key and the roles as first-century culture.
  • Powers: many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians read 6:12 as personal demonic forces; Walter Wink (1935–2012, Naming the Powers, 1984) read the "powers" as also the spirit of institutions and systems.
  • Judge it by: Can a timeless principle be separated from first-century forms? Does the letter's vision of unity survive its social codes?
Mission check

?A new Christian asks why Ephesians spends three chapters describing what God has done before giving a single command. Which answer best reflects the structure of the letter?

In Ephesians the gift always comes first: those "seated in heaven" with Christ (2:6) must still stand firm, in love and in armour, on earth.

Mission 7

Mission 7: Churches split, clash with the law, then help end wars. Does religion divide or reconcile?

Make a guess: Churches split, clash with the law, then help end wars. Does religion divide or reconcile?

Mission 7

Controversy from the start

  • Paul's letters (A2 2) were written into controversy:
  • Galatia: must Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the Law? Paul says no: justification by faith (see Mission 1).
  • Antioch: Peter stops eating with Gentiles under pressure; Paul confronts him (Galatians 2:11–14).
  • Corinth: factions ("I follow Paul", "I follow Apollos", 1 Corinthians 1:12); disputes over food offered to idols (1 Corinthians 8), lawsuits, worship (–b).
  • Jerusalem: "The apostles and the elders were gathered together to see about this matter." (Acts 15:6): the first church council.
  • Synoptic task: link to at least one other unit (e.g. A2 2 Paul, A2 4 Early Church, A2 5 Reformation) and to human experience.
Mission 7Read the source

Division and its cure

> "But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned." (Galatians 2:11, WEBBE)

> "…that there be no divisions amongst you, but that you be perfected together in the same mind and in the same judgement." (1 Corinthians 1:10, WEBBE)

Q1 Does Paul avoid conflict for the sake of unity?

Show answer

No: he confronts Peter openly, because he believes the truth of the gospel is at stake.

Q2 What, then, is the unity Paul wants in Corinth?

Show answer

Agreement in Christ, not loyalty to rival leaders.

  • The tension remains in every age: truth and unity can pull apart.
Mission 7

How the church has responded

  • Councils and creeds: Jerusalem (Acts 15); Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451) defined doctrine against Arianism and other views.
  • Discipline: exclusion of those who refuse correction (1 Corinthians 5:13); later excommunication.
  • Bearing with difference: "accept one who is weak in faith, but not for disputes over opinions" (Romans 14:1).
  • Schism: East and West (1054); the Reformation.
  • Dialogue: the World Council of Churches (1948); Vatican II's decree on ecumenism (1964); the Catholic–Lutheran Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999).
Mission 7

Controversy today

  • Disputes over sexuality and marriage have divided several worldwide churches:
  • Anglican Communion: Lambeth resolution I.10 (1998); the GAFCON movement (2008) of churches dissenting from Western provinces' changes.
  • Methodist: many US congregations left the United Methodist Church (2019–2023).
  • Presbyterian Church in Ireland (2018): ruled that people in same-sex relationships are not eligible for communicant membership, and ended official attendance at the Church of Scotland's General Assembly over its changing position.
  • Others: women's ordination; responses to abuse; the use of church property.
  • Responses: listening processes, conscience clauses, new structures, separation.
Quick check
?Which response to controversy does Romans 14:1 recommend?
Mission 7Evaluate

Is controversy always harmful to religion?

  • Claim: Controversy weakens religion and damages its witness.
  • For: splits multiply churches, waste energy, and cause bitterness; outsiders see division as evidence against the message (compare John 17:21).
  • For: past controversies ended in persecution and war (e.g. the wars of religion after the Reformation).
  • Against: controversy forced clarity: Galatians, Nicaea and the Reformation all defined belief more sharply.
  • Against: debate shows a living faith; Paul himself confronted error.
  • Judgement criteria: essential or secondary matters (Romans 14)? Conflict handled with love or with force? Short-term pain or long-term clarity?
Mission 7

Areas of moral conflict with secular society

  • Secular principles: personal autonomy, the harm principle (J. S. Mill, On Liberty, 1859: the law may restrict liberty only to prevent harm to others), equality law, a neutral state.
  • Areas where many religious believers differ from current law or opinion:
  • Beginning and end of life: abortion (decriminalised in Northern Ireland, 2019); assisted dying.
  • Marriage and sexuality: same-sex marriage (Northern Ireland, 2020).
  • Conscience and freedom: medical conscientious objection; the Ashers Baking Company case (UK Supreme Court, 2018: a business could not be compelled to write a message its owners disagreed with).
  • Education: faith schools, religious education, relationships education.
  • Believers themselves disagree on most of these.
Mission 7

The apostles on the church and the world

  • "Don't be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Romans 12:2): Christian values may differ from society's.
  • "Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities" (Romans 13:1): respect for the state's role.
  • "We must obey God rather than men." (Peter and the apostles, Acts 5:29): limits when a law conflicts with conscience.
  • Paul does not ask Christians to judge outsiders: "those who are outside, God judges" (1 Corinthians 5:13).
  • Debate: should churches campaign to shape law, or only form the lives of their members?
Mission 7Diversity

Five models of Christ and culture

  • H. Richard Niebuhr (1894–1962), Christ and Culture (1951):
  • Christ against culture: withdraw and live differently (e.g. Amish, some Anabaptists).
  • Christ of culture: Christianity fits the best of the culture (liberal Protestantism).
  • Christ above culture: culture is good but needs grace to complete it (Aquinas; much Catholic thought).
  • Christ and culture in paradox: two realms, live in both with tension (Luther).
  • Christ transforming culture: culture is fallen but can be converted (Augustine, Calvin, many social reformers).
  • Each model gives a different answer to "how far should the church oppose secular morality?"
Quick check
?A church urges its members to vote and campaign to change laws, so that society reflects Christian values. Which of Niebuhr's models fits this best?
Mission 7Evaluate

Is conflict with secular society inevitable?

  • Claim: Religion and secular society are bound to clash on morality.
  • For: different foundations: divine command and natural law versus autonomy and consent.
  • For: religious believers see some issues (life, marriage) as matters of truth, not preference; compromise is hard.
  • Against: much secular morality (human dignity, care for the weak, equality) has religious roots; many issues see broad agreement.
  • Against: believers are on every side of these debates; some argue for a plural society with protected conscience.
  • Judgement criteria: which issues? Which believers? Is the aim to win laws or to live faithfully? Can conscience and equality both be protected?
Mission 7Read the source

The ministry of reconciliation

> "But all things are of God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, and gave to us the ministry of reconciliation;" (2 Corinthians 5:18, WEBBE)

> "For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of separation," (Ephesians 2:14, WEBBE)

  • Also: "neither Jew nor Greek, … slave nor free man, … male nor female" (Galatians 3:28); Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus "no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother" (Philemon 1:16).

Q1 Who reconciles first, according to 2 Corinthians 5:18?

Show answer

God, through Christ.

Q2 What task follows for Christians?

Show answer

To carry on a ministry of reconciliation: between people as well as with God; Ephesians 2:14 applies it to Jew and Gentile.

Mission 7

Reconciliation in practice

  • Corrymeela Community (founded 1965 by Rev. Ray Davey): a residential centre on the Antrim coast bringing Protestants and Catholics together.
  • Clonard–Fitzroy Fellowship (1981): a Catholic monastery and a Presbyterian congregation in Belfast praying and studying together (Fr Gerry Reynolds and Rev. Ken Newell).
  • Fr Alec Reid of Clonard helped open the dialogue that led towards the peace process.
  • South Africa: Archbishop Desmond Tutu chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (1996–1998); No Future Without Forgiveness (1999): truth-telling and amnesty, not revenge.
  • Miroslav Volf (b. 1956), Exclusion and Embrace (1996): reconciliation as "embrace", without denying justice.
  • Critique within Christianity: the South African Kairos Document (1985) warned against preaching reconciliation without justice or repentance.
Mission 7Evaluate

Does religion foster reconciliation?

  • Claim: Religion is a force for reconciliation rather than division.
  • For: core texts call for forgiveness and peace (Matthew 5:9; 2 Corinthians 5:18); churches have built trust across divides (Corrymeela, Clonard, the TRC).
  • For: faith gives motives that politics lacks: forgiveness, love of enemies, hope.
  • Against: religious identity marked the sides in Northern Ireland's Troubles and many other conflicts; churches were slow to cross lines.
  • Against: calls to forgive can pressure victims or excuse injustice (the Kairos critique).
  • Judgement criteria: religion as belief or as group identity? Leaders or ordinary members? Peace without justice, or justice without peace?
Mission check

?After a long civil conflict, a church leader urges victims to forgive their attackers at once and "move on", without any public account of what happened or any change in unjust laws. Which criticism would the Kairos Document make?

Christian reconciliation, in its own texts, joins forgiveness to truth and justice. Next synoptic theme: leadership, text and alienation.

Recap

The big ideas

Mission 1

  • Written to Gentile believers in Galatia (South Galatian view: the First Journey churches) after rival teachers demanded circumcision and the Jewish calendar; Paul defends his gospel and apostleship (1:1–2:21).
  • Justification "not by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ" (2:16): Abraham, the curse borne by Christ, the Law as temporary "tutor", "all one in Christ Jesus" (3:28); read differently by Luther, Catholic teaching and the New Perspective (Sanders, Dunn).
  • Freedom for love, not licence (5:1, 13–14); walk by the Spirit; works of the flesh vs fruit of the Spirit; bear one another's burdens.

Mission 2

  • Luther: justification by grace through faith alone; Christ's righteousness imputed; the believer is righteous and sinner at once (Romans 1:17; 5:1; Ephesians 2:8–9; Galatians 2:16).
  • Good works matter as the fruit and evidence of faith, not as a means of earning salvation.

Mission 3

  • Trent (1547): justification is God's free gift, received with cooperating free will; righteousness is infused and grows through works done in grace.
  • Sanders: Judaism was "covenantal nomism"; Paul's dispute over "works of the law" was whether Gentiles must keep the Law to belong (Dunn: "identity markers"); judgement by works stays.

Mission 4

  • Roman Corinth: a rebuilt colony of trade, status and rhetoric; the church founded on the second journey (Acts 18) and written to from Ephesus after reports and a letter.
  • Factions ("I follow Paul… Apollos… Cephas… Christ", 1:12): Paul answers "Is Christ divided?" with the foolishness of the cross, the low status of believers and his own plain preaching.
  • Leaders are servants and stewards; God gives the growth; Christ is the only foundation; the church is God's temple. The teaching targets a status-conscious, mixed, gift-proud audience.

Mission 5

  • Moral living: discipline for the incestuous man (ch. 5); "All things are lawful" answered: the body is a temple of the Spirit, "bought with a price" (6:19–20); mutual duties and the gift of celibacy (ch. 7); idol food: knowledge vs love, care for the weak, flee idolatry (chs 8; 10:14–11:1).
  • Worship: head coverings; rich and poor divided at the Lord's Supper, corrected by the earliest account of its institution (11:23–26); gifts in one body, love as their measure, order (chs 12–14); Sunday collection (16:1–4).
  • Churches differ today over the Supper, gifts, women's roles and discipline; relevance depends on separating principle from application.

Mission 6

  • Ephesus was the centre of Paul's longest mission (Acts 19–20). The letter claims Paul as author; its missing address, style and closeness to Colossians fuel debate (Paul, a disciple, or a circular letter).
  • Chapters 1–3: God's plan to sum up all things in Christ, salvation by grace through faith, Jew and Gentile made one. Chapters 4–6: unity and gifts in the church, the new life in the world, a reciprocal household code, the armour of God.
  • Its value then (one Church, identity, courage) and relevance now (unity, reconciliation, marriage, the "powers") are both debated, especially the household code.

Mission 7

  • Controversy runs from Paul's letters (Antioch, Corinth, Jerusalem) to today; churches respond with councils, discipline, tolerance of difference, schism or dialogue.
  • Moral conflict with secular society (life, marriage, conscience, education) depends on foundations and on the model of church and culture (Niebuhr).
  • Paul's "ministry of reconciliation" inspires peace work (Corrymeela, Clonard, the TRC), but critics warn that reconciliation needs truth and justice.
